title: Modular Application Architecture and Separation of Concerns
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and behaviour of Modular Application Architecture and Separation of Concerns.
Choose an appropriate modular application architecture and separation of concerns technique for a Python application.
Interpret representative code and output involving modular application architecture and separation of concerns.
Identify limitations and failure modes for modular application architecture and separation of concerns.
Apply the concepts in maintainable Python code.

understand.concept: Application architecture separates responsibilities so that domain rules, data access, user interaction and external integrations can evolve independently. Modules should expose small, intentional interfaces and avoid circular dependencies. A clear dependency direction keeps core business rules independent of infrastructure details.
understand.whyItMatters: A modular design makes changes safer, tests more focused and code easier for multiple developers to understand.
understand.analogy: A well-run workshop has separate stations for design, assembly, inspection and shipping, with clear handoffs.
understand.analogyLimit: Dividing code into many files does not automatically create good architecture; boundaries must reflect real responsibilities.
understand.summary: Modular Application Architecture and Separation of Concerns develops practical application engineering skills for Python projects.

explain.narrative:
## Organize around responsibilities
Separate domain logic from input/output. Keep functions that calculate or decide business rules independent of HTTP, database and UI details. Put persistence behind a repository interface and external services behind adapters. Avoid circular imports and avoid modules that do too many unrelated jobs. Start with a simple structure and introduce additional layers only when they solve a real coupling or testing problem.

examples.title: Separate a calculation from output
examples.code:
def line_total(price: float, quantity: int) -> float:
    return price * quantity
result = line_total(12.5, 3)
print(result)
examples.explanation: The calculation has no dependency on a terminal, database or web framework.

examples.title: Represent a domain value
examples.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Money:
    amount: int
    currency: str
price = Money(1250, 'INR')
print(price.currency, price.amount)
examples.explanation: A domain record captures a concept independently of persistence.

examples.title: Keep presentation outside a rule
examples.explanation: The rule returns a value; presentation formats it separately.

examples.title: Expose a small module interface
examples.code:
__all__ = ['calculate_tax']
def calculate_tax(amount: int) -> int:
    return amount // 10
print(calculate_tax(250))
examples.explanation: An explicit export list documents the intended public interface.

examples.title: Compose independent steps
examples.explanation: Small functions can be composed into a workflow while retaining distinct responsibilities.

practise.guidedTask: Split a small order-processing example into domain calculation, repository interface and presentation. Keep business rules free of database imports.
practise.independentTask: Draw module dependencies for a CLI inventory app and identify any circular or inward infrastructure dependency.
hints: Keep core business rules independent of I/O.
Use modules to group related responsibilities.
Do not add layers without a concrete reason.
practise.challenge: Refactor a monolithic expense-report script into domain, repository, service and CLI modules with tests for the domain layer.
validationCriteria: The concept and intended use are accurately explained.
All examples execute with the documented output on Python 3.13.
Application boundaries and dependency responsibilities are correctly identified.
Limitations and operational or security implications are explained.

questions.answer: In code independent of infrastructure details
options: In code independent of infrastructure details

questions.prompt: Does splitting code into many files guarantee good architecture?
questions.explanation: Good architecture depends on meaningful responsibility boundaries, not file count.
